title: Lehna becomes Angad
hookLine: Nanak names Lehna his successor and calls him Angad, part of my own body

lines: THE GURU WAS WATCHING SOMEONE ELSE.
cards: Guru Nanak had two grown sons. The elder, Sri Chand, was deeply devout, an ascetic who had renounced ordinary life. The younger, Lakhmi Das, was a householder with a family.
When a founder steps down, the next in line can seem obvious, the way the eldest son takes over the family shop. Either son would have been the obvious choice.
But for years Nanak had been watching someone else: the trader who carried the wet grass, cleared the ditch and fished the bowl out of dirty water.
So step back a little in time, to a few months before the flowers, and the day Nanak made his choice.

teach.h: THE TEACHER BOWED TO THE STUDENT.
teach.b: Tradition says Nanak placed a coconut and five copper coins before Lehna and bowed to him. The teacher bowed to the student. Then he gave him a new name: Angad.

teach.h: ANG — A LIMB, PART OF THE BODY.
teach.b: Ang means a limb, a part of the body, so Angad is often explained as part of my own body. This man isn't my replacement, the Guru was saying; he's me, continued.
A ballad in the scripture, sung by two of the Gurus' musicians, Satta and Balvand, says it plainly: the light was the same, the way was the same; the king had only changed his body.
That's the Sikh understanding of the ten Gurus. Not ten teachers with ten different messages, but one light passed from one body to the next, like a flame lit from a flame.
That's why the Gurus whose hymns are in the scripture signed them not with their own names but with Nanak's. The word takes one more turn. Ang also names the pages of the Sikh scripture.
You don't say page 360 of the Guru Granth Sahib; you say Ang 360. Each page is a limb of the Guru.

teach.h: ANG — EVERY PAGE OF THE SCRIPTURE.
teach.b: The word that named the second Guru now names every page of the book Sikhs call their Guru today. And notice: Nanak didn't choose by blood. He chose the one who had become a servant.
The light went to the one who could carry it, and it's still traveling.

how: Sikhs understand the ten Gurus as one light passing through ten bodies, and they refer to the pages of the Guru Granth Sahib as angs, limbs of the Guru; Guru Angad's accession is remembered each year.

he chose Lehna and renamed him Angad.
Sikhs call the pages of their scripture angs
each page is a limb of the Guru.
the Gurus in the scripture signed their hymns with their own names
they signed as Nanak: one light, passed from body to body.

games.q: you're Guru Nanak, choosing who will lead after you. you have two devout sons, and one tireless disciple. what do you do?
o: bow to the disciple and give him a new name.
games.why: tradition says Nanak bowed to Lehna and named him Angad, part of my own body. the light went to the servant.

practice: Think of something you care about: a skill, a family recipe, a way of doing your job, a value your parents gave you. Then see the face of whoever might carry it after you, a child, a colleague, a friend, a student.
If nobody comes to mind, notice that too, and wonder who it might be.

wordCard.voice: Ang. A limb, a part of the body; inside the name Angad, and the word Sikhs use for every page of their scripture. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: ang, a limb or part of the body; Angad, part of me; and each page of the Guru Granth Sahib.
